content:
Earlier this year, when Apple launched the MacBook Neo, the personal computer market was clearly caught off guard. Although the notebook's aggressive pricing strategy has since been adjusted in response to market conditions, it took the Windows camp competitors several months to successively reveal their counterattack products. HP joined the battle today with a new notebook featuring an OLED display, also starting at US$699 — though there are quite a few caveats behind the price tag.

Overall, the HP OmniBook 5 14 looks like a colourful budget version of the MacBook Neo body, paired with the more refined, understated green and blue tones of the Apple iPad Air lineup. Beneath the 14-inch display, the chassis is just 11.77mm thick and weighs only 2.56 pounds — perfect timing for back-to-school shopping, but for some reason HP missed that window. The real highlight of this machine is that 14-inch display — at this price point, you would normally only see IPS panels, but this time there are two OLED options to choose from, with details to be announced later. Each side of the chassis has a full-function USB-C port and a headphone jack; open the lid and you will find an FHD camera with Windows Hello support.

In terms of hardware specifications, HP says the notebook supports up to an Intel Core 7 processor, but the model shown only came in a single configuration. The battery life on the spec sheet is quite impressive — up to 42 hours of local video playback (battery capacity not listed) — though to be fair, local video playback tests do not necessarily reflect real-world usage. HP mentioned that the machine is compatible with its 65W GaN mini charger, which is expected to be included in the box. Beyond that, the known specs include dual microphones and audio tuned by Poly Studio; if you feel there is still a lot of information missing, you are definitely not alone.

First of all, the processor model for the US$700 version of this notebook has yet to be revealed, making direct comparison with Apple's A18 Pro difficult. HP also chose not to disclose any storage or memory configuration information — not even "up to" figures — which directly reflects the immense pressure the PC market is under amid the current memory supply crunch. Even the most eye-catching selling point comes with a fatal trade-off: HP spent considerable time at the launch event giving a lengthy description of that 2.5K OLED display, but that version will not ship until March 2027. The model going on sale at Best Buy at the end of this month features a 2K OLED display, but the brightness drops sharply from 650 nits to just 300 nits.

Given all the unspecified details above, and some of the disappointing answers, if HP has still managed to pique your interest, please stay tuned for more information to be released before the product officially goes on sale.
